extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians writing research papers and expository articles (graduate students, researchers, authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical style and clarity guidelines for writing mathematics: structuring proofs and statements, LaTeX usage, citation habits, and nitpicky grammatical/formal conventions aimed at improving readability and correctness of math papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain non-immediate claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim does not follow immediately from the previous sentence alone, explain what it does follow from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give explicit links such as “Combining the previous two sentences shows that...”, or cite the supporting result: “By Lemma 8.3, ...”.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify justification for each claim in multi-claim sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sentence contains more than one claim, make clear which reason is the justification for each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In chains of equalities, indicate the reason for each equality, e.g. place a reason before/after the chain or use align environment with a reason at the right of each line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure reader knows why each claim is true by sentence end
rubrics_metrics.description: A reader reaching the period of a sentence should know why each claim up to that point is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the proof of a claim will only come after the period, signal this with phrasing like “, as we now explain”, or place the claim into a formal construction such as a lemma with a subsequent proof environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break up long arguments into lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Break up long arguments by making parts of them into lemmas, even if the lemmas are used only once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to minimize what a reader must keep in mind at one time, freeing cognitive load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate which results are used later
rubrics_metrics.description: If a section contains several theorems, propositions, and lemmas, but only one is needed in subsequent sections, mention this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointing out which statements are important later helps readers focus and reduces memory burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make quantifiers unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear whether statements are for all or there exists; avoid ambiguous compact notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of “We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S for x ∈ R” or “We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S, x ∈ R.” write either “We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S for all x ∈ R.” or “We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S for some x ∈ R.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate where hypotheses are used in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should usually indicate where the hypotheses are being used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly point out the step(s) that use each hypothesis so the logical dependence is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give precise citations (theorem/page numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing a book or article, include a theorem number or page number unless you mean to cite the entire work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit the specific locator only in rare cases when the whole work is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite arXiv/preprints with version or date and URL
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing an arXiv preprint, include the version number or precise date; for other preprints give the URL and manuscript date or date downloaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps readers find the exact version you referenced even if newer versions appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not cite 'forthcoming' without a public preprint
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite 'forthcoming work' only if there is a publicly available preprint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpublished announcements can discourage others and be misleading if the work never appears; see AMS ethical guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep theorem statements short
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep theorem statements short and place definitions before the theorem where they are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long, overloaded theorem statements by providing necessary definitions ahead of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep sentences short
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep sentences short; combine sentences only if it clarifies logic or they are closely related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine with ', and' or a semicolon only when it improves clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: String together chains of equalities/inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: If an argument involves combining several equalities, string them together in one chain (in correct order) to leverage transitivity; same for inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes logic easier to follow by using familiar transitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction should get to main theorems quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction to an article should get to new and interesting theorems as soon as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's OK to postpone definitions to a later Notation section if standard; refer readers to that section from the introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove easier parts first when a proof breaks into parts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof breaks into parts, do the easier parts first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering subproofs by ease can clarify structure and motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start induction at convenient base case
rubrics_metrics.description: Start induction arguments with base case n = 0 instead of n = 1 if it is easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the base case that makes the induction cleanest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid informal abbreviations in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use abbreviations like WLOG, iff, and s.t. in formal writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those abbreviations are primarily for blackboard use and are inappropriate in polished papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical symbols outside formal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use logical symbols such as ∃ and ∀ unless writing about formal logic and they appear in formulas; write 'there exists' or 'for all' in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See CMOS 12.5 for recommended practices; spell out existential/universal quantifiers in running text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence subject must be a grammatical unit (not split by formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a sentence or clause cannot consist of words outside a formula together with a fraction of the formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of splitting the predicate from the subject across the formula, include the formula as part of the subject and complete the sentence, e.g. “For a quadratic polynomial ax^2 + bx + c, the discriminant ∆ equals b^2 − 4ac.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid starting sentences with a symbol; such fragments should be rewritten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of standalone symbol sentences like “H denotes the Sylow p-subgroup of G.”, include a preceding clause so the sentence begins with words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contractions in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid contractions such as “don’t” in formal writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the full forms ('do not') in papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid saying 'clear' without explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually when people write that something is 'clear', it is because they do not know the proof or could not find a good way to write it; if it really is clear you don't need to say so; if not, give some reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide at least a hint or a few words motivating why something holds instead of just labeling it 'clear'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize use of ', where ...' after notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize the ', where ...' construction where explanations of notation come after the notation is used; define variables before they are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to introduce definitions/notation prior to use to avoid delayed explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer to theorems by number not relative position
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to theorems by number instead of writing 'the previous theorem' or 'the proposition above'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbered references are clearer and robust to editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a single numbering system for theorem-like environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a single numbering system for all theorems, lemmas, etc., instead of having conflicting numbering (e.g., both Theorem 1.1 and Lemma 1.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Use LaTeX 
ewtheorem setup (or amsthm) to number environments consistently so statements are easier to find and citation errors are reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use DeclareMathOperator for named operators
rubrics_metrics.description: To get correct typesetting for operators like Gal, declare them in the preamble with \DeclareMathOperator and use the declared command in the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \DeclareMathOperator{\Gal}{Gal} in the preamble and then \Gal in the text to get proper spacing and font.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \hfill before enumerate to prevent misalignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \hfill before \begin{enumerate} if necessary to prevent misalignment of the first item in displayed theorem-like labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents awkward indentation where items (a),(b),(c) appear misaligned under a theorem header.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use f \colon X \to Y for correct colon spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of f : X \to Y use f \colon X \to Y for appropriate spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields more correct typographic spacing in math mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fullpage package to fit more text
rubrics_metrics.description: Try \usepackage{fullpage} in the preamble to fit more on a page without setting margins manually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple way to adjust page layout without manual margin fiddling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use microtype package to reduce bad line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Try \usepackage{microtype} just before \begin{document} to allow LaTeX to adjust spacing between characters to reduce bad line breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improves justification and typography subtly and automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider colonequals package for := spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have mastered other aspects, try \usepackage{colonequals} and use \colonequals for well-spaced := symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare := and \colonequals carefully for spacing and style consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'so that' vs 'such that'
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference is that 'so that' conveys purpose while 'such that' indicates a condition; choose appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If replacing 'so that' with 'in order that' makes it sound wrong, you probably meant 'such that'. Example: Do not write 'An abelian group is a group so that every two elements commute.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'A, so B' for logical implication
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are indicating a logical implication between A and B, write 'A, so B' instead of 'A, so that B' or 'A, and so B'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred concise phrasing for logical consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place 'only' close to the word it modifies
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'only' should be placed as close as possible to the word it modifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misplaced 'only' can change meaning; see referenced examples [Kil07].

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper phrasing for 'Given' constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of 'Given g an element of G' write 'Given an element g of G'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeps grammatical structure clear and conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize 'Theorem' etc. when referring by number
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to a theorem (or proposition, section, etc.) by number, capitalize the word 'Theorem'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'By Section 3.4 and Theorem 5.6, the proposition holds.' 'By Faltings’s theorem, X(Q) is finite.' (note capitalization guidance applies when referencing by number)

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain punctuation when displaying formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Displaying a formula does not change the punctuation required in the surrounding sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Don't drop terminal punctuation; e.g. write 'By Theorem 3.2, we have

Gal(L/K) ≅ Z/2Z × Z/2Z.

' rather than leaving the formula unpunctuated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Assume that' for clause starts unless the noun unit is standalone
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 'Assume that G is a finite group.' rather than 'Assume G is a finite group.'; exceptions include 'Assume Hypothesis A.' or 'Assume n ≥ 1.' where the following unit serves as a noun phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same rules apply to 'Suppose'. See [Wes15] for more details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct decade punctuation (1980s not 1980's)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 'the 1980s', not 'the 1980's'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow CMOS 9.34 for decade formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow punctuation rules for i.e. and e.g.
rubrics_metrics.description: I.e. and e.g. should be followed by a comma; if they separate full sentences, they should be preceded by a semicolon rather than a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe sentence-level punctuation conventions around abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize parentheses use; omit where conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize use of parentheses; e.g. log x is better than log(x); omit parentheses in sin 2x but include them in sin(x + y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parentheses only when necessary to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid centered dot for multiplication usually
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually it is not necessary to use a centered dot or other symbol for multiplication; write (n+1)(n+2) rather than (n+1)·(n+2) or (n+1)×(n+2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: when both factors are numbers, juxtaposition is confusing, so use 3 · 7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit filler phrases like 'We remark that' and 'Note that'
rubrics_metrics.description: Filler words such as 'We remark that' and 'Note that' should be omitted except when their absence would produce a sentence starting with a symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary lead-ins unless they serve a typographic/grammatical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't restate conclusion redundantly at proof end
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof ends with an end-of-proof symbol, it is not necessary to write 'This concludes the proof.' or 'Thus we are done.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The end-of-proof symbol suffices to indicate closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use slash for fractions in exponents/subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Fractions in exponents or subscripts should use the slash instead of being stacked vertically; write x^{3/2}, not x^{3/2} with stacked fraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow CMOS 12.47 for recommended inline fraction formatting in exponents/subscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write sequences with parentheses not set braces
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as ordered tuples are written (2,3,5) instead of {2,3,5}, a sequence should be written (a_i)_{i≥0} instead of {a_i}_{i≥0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conventional parentheses to denote ordered sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hyphenate common 'non' prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefix 'non' does not need a hyphen in common words like nonempty, nonnegative, nonsingular, nontrivial, nonzero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow CMOS 7.85 on 'non' prefix hyphenation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most numbers in math papers should be numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Most numbers in math papers should be written as numerals instead of words; exception: single-digit counting numbers used only as counting words may be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example exception: 'These two genus 2 curves are isomorphic.' Note: some authors spell small numbers as words in more situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'since' over 'as' for 'because' meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Technically it is OK to use 'as' as a synonym for 'since', but this use of 'as' sounds stilted and can be ambiguous; prefer 'since'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sentences like 'As x does not tend to +∞, the expression e^x is bounded.' which can be confusing.
